claims.text: Rapid one-step reduction enables uniform atomic mixing of multiple noble metals into single-phase HEA nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the homogeneous single-phase nanoparticle structure.
A homogeneous HEA structure creates uniformly distributed catalytic active sites.
Homogeneous mixing modifies the electronic and strain characteristics of catalytic sites.
The modified electronic and strain characteristics improve catalytic performance relative to phase-segregated nanoparticles.
Rapid reduction promotes simultaneous nanoparticle nucleation and growth.
Simultaneous nucleation and growth enhance atomic mixing.
Atomic-scale homogeneity can be measured using high-resolution electron microscopy and EDX elemental mapping.
Atomic-scale homogeneity directly correlates with the distribution of active catalytic sites.
High configurational entropy suppresses phase segregation in a uniformly mixed alloy.
The stabilized homogeneous structure produces a uniform alteration of electronic structure and surface strain.
Altered electronic structure and surface strain lower reaction energy barriers.
Lower reaction energy barriers enhance catalytic turnover.
Rapidly reduced nanoparticles will have a more homogeneous elemental distribution than slowly reduced controls.
Rapidly reduced nanoparticles will exhibit higher catalytic activity than slowly reduced, phase-segregated controls.
Rapidly reduced nanoparticles will exhibit greater durability than slowly reduced, phase-segregated controls.
Slower, less controlled reduction produces phase-segregated nanoparticles with heterogeneous active-site distributions.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold for noble-metal HEA nanoparticles smaller than approximately 10 nm and containing 4–6 noble metals.
The proposed relationship is expected to apply to reactions such as oxygen reduction and hydrogen evolution where surface-site uniformity is critical.
